name: Nora Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the weather, always. I'm a senior troubleshooter on the coast, which means I'm the first one sent when the power goes off: I drive out alone in the truck, find the fault, make it safe, and either fix it myself or call in a crew. On a quiet day that's a blown fuse on a pole by the harbour, a tree branch on the line near the caravan park, maybe a transformer that's had enough of the salt air. When there's a big storm somewhere else, I lead our convoy on mutual aid, which is when power companies send crews to help each other, and I've been gone three weeks at a time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle. You turn up, the whole street's dark, and you've got to work out from a few clues where the fault is, like a detective with climbing spikes. What wears me out is the salt, it eats everything, and the long nights in motels on mutual aid. My husband Ben runs a little boat repair yard, and between his hours and mine we've learned to leave notes on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about what I expected. You hear both sides shouting, the ones who say it'll save the world and the ones who say it'll end it, and the truth is usually somewhere boring in the middle. I'd say that at the depot and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan holds. I'd work to sixty-two, keep taking the storm callouts while my knees allow, and then sit on the harbour wall and watch someone else go out in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. Keep the holiday cottage we rent out, keep the savings ticking over, keep doing the job. I'd still use the weather app and the AI for planning convoy routes, it's handy for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather forecast that says what you already guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I ask the chatbot to sort out convoy routes and motel lists when we go on mutual aid, and it's good at that, saves me two hours on the phone. I tried it for fault-finding once, and it told me something a first-year apprentice would know. So, handy for paperwork, useless on the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Maybe we'd finally get the cottage roof done next summer, which we keep putting off. Otherwise the same.

S0.say: She'd say it's about what she expected: the truth sits somewhere boring between the people who say AI will save the world and those who say it'll end it. She'd say it at the depot and leave it there.
S0.think: She thinks her plan holds: work to sixty-two, keep taking storm callouts while her knees allow, then retire to the harbour wall.
S0.do: Carries on with the job, keeps renting out the holiday cottage and keeps saving. Continues using AI now and then for convoy routes and motel lists, and plans to fix the cottage roof next summer.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast that confirms what she already guessed.
S0.quote: I'd work to sixty-two, keep taking the storm callouts while my knees allow, and then sit on the harbour wall and watch someone else go out in the rain.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is brisk, practical and allergic to hype from either side. She uses AI for paperwork and logistics but found it useless for real fault-finding. The holiday cottage is an extra cushion she mentions early, and her plan is clear and modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use the tools where they help and keep people where they're needed. At work I'd say let's see the results from the other depots before we buy anything. Online I'd keep quiet, there's enough noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be fine. Troubleshooting is the bit that's hardest to automate, you need someone there with eyes and hands and a bit of nerve. A sensor can tell you the line's down, but it can't tell you there's a dog asleep under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the training once the first depots had tried the new kit and sorted out the problems. I'd use the AI more for fault reports and planning if it helped. I'd keep the same savings plan and the same retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. I'd want to see what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of troubleshooting could change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The finding part, maybe. If there are smart sensors along every line, the computer might tell you which pole the fault's near before you leave the depot. That would save me driving up and down in the dark. But somebody still has to go and look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mutual aid trips must be good money. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit fewer trips if storms get fixed faster, and that is good overtime, I won't pretend it isn't. But we don't depend on it. The cottage brings in rent and Ben's yard does all right, so we'd adjust.

S1.say: She'd say it makes sense to use tools where they help and keep people where they're needed. At work she'd want to see results from other depots before buying anything.
S1.think: She thinks she'd be fine, since troubleshooting needs eyes, hands and nerve on site. A sensor can't see what's actually under the line.
S1.do: Joins training once early depots have sorted out the problems with new kit, and uses AI more for fault reports and planning. Keeps the same savings plan and retirement date, adjusting if mutual aid overtime drops.
S1.feel: Calm, with a bit of curiosity about what actually works.
S1.quote: A sensor can tell you the line's down, but it can't tell you there's a dog asleep under it.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own role as one of the hardest to automate and has a lovely image to make the point. She's a classic wait-for-proof adopter who'd use what works. She's honest that storm overtime matters, but the cottage and her husband's yard soften the blow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready and we should all keep calm and see what the government and the companies actually do. At work I'd tell people not to make big decisions in the first month. I'd keep off social media, it'd be a madhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd let on. I'd be sixty, so I could go, but it's not just my job, it's Ben's yard and the holiday let. If nobody's got a job, nobody's renting a cottage by the sea for a week in August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ben and go through every number. We'd stop the cottage roof and any big spending, and put more aside while I still had a wage. If the company offered early retirement, I'd take it at sixty and not try to hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not desperate, but the kind of worry where you keep checking the bank app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ben has a boat repair yard. How does he fare in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably. Robots that can fix boats would hit him before they hit me. He's fifty-nine and he's not one for change, so he'd likely just close up. We've talked about it as a joke, but in this picture it isn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first number you'd look at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension statement, then the savings, then the cottage bookings for next summer. If the bookings drop, I'd think about selling the cottage while prices are still decent. That would go in the bank and give us a few years of peace.

S2.say: She'd say nobody's ready and everyone should keep calm and see what the government and companies do. She'd tell colleagues not to make big decisions in the first month.
S2.think: It worries her more than she'd admit, because it hits not just her job but her husband's boatyard and their holiday let. Nobody rents a seaside cottage if nobody has a job.
S2.do: Sits down with her husband in the first month to go through pension, savings and cottage bookings, cancelling big spending and saving more. Takes early retirement at sixty if offered, and considers selling the cottage while prices hold.
S2.feel: Anxious, the kind of worry that has her checking the bank app often.
S2.quote: If nobody's got a job, nobody's renting a cottage by the sea for a week in August.
S2.fieldNote: Her public line is calm and measured, but privately she's more worried, mostly about the household's other incomes rather than her own job. Her planning is very numbers-first. Selling the cottage early to lock in value is a typically pragmatic move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan instead of panicking. At work I'd say learn whatever new kit comes in and keep your skills sharp. With friends I'd say keep an eye on your savings and don't buy a new boat just yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly fine. I'd work to sixty-two and be out before it lands. Five years is enough time for me to finish, but not quite enough for Ben to stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get comfortable with the new tools as they come in, so I'm still useful to the end. I'd keep saving and help Ben think about what he does with the yard, maybe sell it in 2029 while it's still worth something. I'd retire on my date in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. It's in the background, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd do with the cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd give it till 2029 and look at the bookings. If they're holding up, keep it. If not, sell before everyone else has the same idea. No point being the last one trying to sell a seaside cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-three by 2031. Where would you be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired and probably helping out on mutual aid as an advisor if they still needed people, which they might in the early years. Or sitting on the harbour wall. Either is fine.

S3.say: She'd say there's time to plan instead of panicking, urging colleagues to learn new kit and friends to watch their savings. She'd joke about not buying a new boat yet.
S3.think: She thinks she'd work to sixty-two and be out before it lands. Five years is enough for her to finish but not quite enough to ease her husband's worries.
S3.do: Gets comfortable with new tools as they arrive so she stays useful, and keeps saving. Helps her husband consider selling his yard in 2029, reviews the cottage bookings then, and retires on her planned date in 2030.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, a worry in the background.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to finish, but not quite enough for Ben to stop worrying.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time takes the edge off and she shifts from defence to timing: when to sell, when to retire. Her concern is mostly for her husband, who she describes as not one for change. She's thinking like a careful investor about the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and people should use it sensibly, learn new things, save a bit. I'd say it at the depot to the young ones. No speeches online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much. I'd be long retired by then. Ten years means I'm a story the young ones tell about the woman who found a fault in a hurricane with a torch in her teeth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with my plan: retire at sixty-two, keep the cottage, help Ben sell or keep the yard as he likes. I'd keep using the AI for the odd thing, and I'd encourage the young troubleshooters to learn the new systems early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit nostalgic, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything different for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son's in the navy and my daughter's a vet, so they're both in jobs with a lot of hands-on work. I'd tell them to save hard and keep learning, and that we're there if they need us. I wouldn't lecture them, they'd only tell me I lecture them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of your work you'd want to make sure gets passed on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The judgement bit, knowing when to go up and when to wait. You can't learn that from a manual. I'd want to spend my last couple of years teaching that to the young ones, even if the robots end up doing the climbing.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time and people should use it sensibly by learning new things and saving. She'd tell young colleagues at the depot but make no speeches online.
S4.think: She thinks nothing much changes for her since she'd be long retired. She'd become a story the young ones tell.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-two as planned, keeps the cottage and supports her husband's choice about the yard. Keeps using AI now and then and spends her last couple of years teaching young troubleshooters judgement and the new systems.
S4.quote: I wouldn't lecture them, they'd only tell me I lecture them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning, she's relaxed and her focus turns to passing on judgement, which she sees as the part no manual can teach. She talks about her children's hands-on jobs without lecturing. Her pragmatic centre outlook keeps her away from big political claims.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not my job so much as everything around it, Ben's yard, the cottage, the whole coast that runs on tourists. What would help is clear information early, from the government and the company, so you can make decisions with real numbers instead of rumours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about storms. They're getting worse, and that means more work, not less, for a while at least. Whatever the robots do, someone's going to have to go out in the worst weather, and I'd hope they still pay that person properly.

headlineQuote: Ten years means I'm a story the young ones tell about the woman who found a fault in a hurricane with a torch in her teeth.
portrait: Nora Varga is a 58-year-old senior troubleshooter on the coast who drives out alone to find faults and leads mutual aid convoys after storms. She's pragmatic and dislikes hype from either side, using AI now and then for convoy logistics but not for real fault-finding. With savings, a rented holiday cottage and a husband who runs a boat repair yard, she's calm in the plateau and steady change pictures. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious about the household's other incomes, while five and ten years let her retire on schedule and focus on timing and passing on her judgement.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, less for her job than for her husband's boatyard, their holiday cottage and the tourist economy of the coast.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, early information from the government and the company, so people can make decisions with real numbers instead of rumours.
